## Overview and Intuition

**Interrupted Time Series (ITS)**

- **Study design**: Quasi-experimental evaluation design
- **Goal**: Determine intervention led to a statistically significant change in an outcome. 

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Setup Parameters & Time Vector
set.seed(42)
t_max <- 24
t_int <- 12  # Intervention point (T0)

time <- 1:t_max
intervention <- ifelse(time > t_int, 1, 0)
time_after <- ifelse(time > t_int, time - t_int, 0)

# True parameters: Y = b0 + b1*T + b2*D + b3*P + e
b0 <- 15     # Baseline intercept
b1 <- 1.2    # Baseline slope
b2 <- 14     # Immediate level jump
b3 <- -0.4   # Post-intervention slope change (trend moderates/levels off)

mu_observed <- b0 + b1 * time + b2 * intervention + b3 * time_after
y_observed <- mu_observed + rnorm(t_max, mean = 0, sd = 1.1)

# Counterfactual trajectory (what would have happened without intervention)
counterfactual <- b0 + b1 * time

df <- data.frame(
  Time = time,
  Outcome = y_observed,
  Intervention = factor(intervention, labels = c("Pre", "Post")),
  Counterfactual = counterfactual
)

# 2. Key Coordinates for Annotations
cf_at_int <- b0 + b1 * t_int
post_at_int <- cf_at_int + b2

# 3. Build ggplot
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Time, y = Outcome)) +
  # Intervention threshold line
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_int + 0.5, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.8) +
  
  # Counterfactual line (post-intervention projection)
  geom_segment(
    aes(x = t_int + 0.5, y = b0 + b1 * (t_int + 0.5),
        xend = t_max, yend = b0 + b1 * t_max),
    linetype = "dashed", color = "#D95F02", linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Pre-intervention fitted regression line
  geom_smooth(
    data = filter(df, Time <= t_int),
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
    color = "#1B9E77", linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  
  # Post-intervention fitted regression line
  geom_smooth(
    data = filter(df, Time > t_int),
    method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
    color = "#7570B3", linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  
  # Observed data points
  geom_point(aes(color = Intervention), size = 2.8, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pre" = "#1B9E77", "Post" = "#7570B3"), guide = "none") +
  
  # Level jump arrow & label
  annotate(
    "segment",
    x = t_int + 0.5, xend = t_int + 0.5,
    y = b0 + b1 * (t_int + 0.5), yend = b0 + b1 * (t_int + 0.5) + b2,
    arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
    color = "#E7298A", linewidth = 0.9
  ) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = t_int + 0.7, y = b0 + b1 * (t_int + 0.5) + (b2 / 2),
    label = "paste('Immediate Level Change (', beta[2], ')')",
    parse = TRUE,
    hjust = 0, size = 3.6, fontface = "bold", color = "#E7298A",
    fill = "white", label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  
  # Text labels for trends
  annotate(
    "text", x = 6, y = b0 + b1 * 6 + 4.5,
    label = "paste('Pre-Intervention Trend (', beta[1], ')')",
    parse = TRUE,
    color = "#1B9E77", fontface = "bold", size = 3.8
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 19, y = (b0 + b1 * 19 + b2 + b3 * (19 - t_int)) + 3.8,
    label = "paste('Observed Post Trend (', beta[1] + beta[3], ')')",
    parse = TRUE,
    color = "#7570B3", fontface = "bold", size = 3.8
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = 20.5, y = b0 + b1 * 20.5 - 2.8,
    label = "Projected Counterfactual\n(Expected path without policy)",
    color = "#D95F02", fontface = "italic", size = 3.4, lineheight = 0.9
  ) +
  annotate(
    "text", x = t_int + 0.5, y = min(df$Outcome) - 1.5,
    label = "paste('Intervention (', italic(T)[0], ')')",
    parse = TRUE,
    color = "gray30", fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, vjust = 1
  ) +
  
  # Scales & Clean Theme
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, t_max, by = 2), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.05))) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.08))) +
  labs(
    title = "Interrupted Time Series Analysis (Segmented Regression)",
    subtitle = expression(paste("Model: ", italic(Y[t]), " = ", beta[0], " + ", beta[1], italic(T), " + ", beta[2], italic(D), " + ", beta[3], italic(P), " + ", epsilon[t])),
    x = "Time (t)",
    y = "Outcome (Y)"
  ) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 14)),
    axis.line = element_line(arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.12, "inches"))),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 15, r = 20, b = 15, l = 15)
  )

# Display
print(p)
```

## The Statistical Model

The standard segmented regression equation fitted in SPSS is:

$$
Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_t + \beta_2 D_t + \beta_3 P_t + \epsilon_t
$$

|  Variable Name  | Coding Rule | Meaning |
| :--- | :---- | :---- |
| **`Time`** ($T_t$) Continuous Time | $1, 2, 3, \dots, N$ | Baseline pre-intervention slope per time unit ($\beta_1$). |
| **`Intervention`** ($D_t$) Level Shift | $0$ before intervention; $1$ after intervention | Immediate vertical jump or drop right after the policy begins ($\beta_2$). |
| **`Time_Post`** ($P_t$) Trend Shift | $0$ before intervention; $1, 2, 3, \dots$ after intervention | Difference between pre- and post-intervention slopes ($\beta_3$). |

## Interpretation of ITS

ITS compares the 

- **Observed post-intervention trajectory** against a 
- **Projected counterfactual trajectory** (what would have happened if the pre-intervention trend had simply continued unchanged).

IF an internvetion does not work at all.

- $\beta_2 = 0$: The intervention does not have immediate effect on the observation
- $\beta_3 = 0$: The intervention does not change the growth rate of the observation

## Regression diagnostics

**Generalizability**

- ITS falls into common generalied linear model (GLM), using in the logistic, poisson, negtive binomial regression is possibile.

**Diagnostic**

- Common regression diagnostic applies
- **Samples are correlated temporally**
  - The observation on $t_1$ is correlated with $t_0$ and so on so forth
  - Violating the assumption the independent sample asumption
  - Durbin-Watson test statistic is $< 1.5$: Adding autoregressive errors

## 3. Preparing the Data in SPSS (No Coding Required)

Example dataset: Regionalization and Outcomes of Lung Cancer Surgery in Ontario, Canada, prepared by Changing Use of Surgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Thika Hospital, Kenya: A Quality Improvement Intervention with an Interrupted Time Series Design


Suppose you have monthly data for $N = 36$ months on hospital-acquired infections, with an infection control policy implemented at **Month 19**.

### Step 1: Create the Baseline Time Variable (`Time`)
If your file does not already have a sequence index from $1$ to $N$:
1. Go to **Transform > Compute Variable...**
2. In **Target Variable**, type: `Time`
3. In **Numeric Expression**, type: `$CASENUM`
4. Click **OK**.

### Step 2: Create the Intervention Indicator (`Intervention`)
This dummy variable marks the immediate level jump.
1. Go to **Transform > Compute Variable...**
2. In **Target Variable**, type: `Intervention`
3. In **Numeric Expression**, type: `Time >= 19`
4. Click **OK**.  
   *(SPSS evaluates logical expressions as $1$ for True and $0$ for False).*

### Step 3: Create the Post-Intervention Time Variable (`Time_Post`)
This continuous variable captures the slope change.
1. Go to **Transform > Compute Variable...**
2. In **Target Variable**, type: `Time_Post`
3. In **Numeric Expression**, type: `0`
4. Click **OK**.
5. Re-open **Transform > Compute Variable...**
6. Keep **Target Variable** as: `Time_Post`
7. In **Numeric Expression**, type: `Time - 18`
8. Click the **If...** button at the bottom:
   * Select **Include if case satisfies condition**.
   * Enter: `Time >= 19`
   * Click **Continue**.
9. Click **OK** and confirm replacement.

### Expected Data View

| Month (Label) | `Infection_Rate` ($Y$) | `Time` ($T$) | `Intervention` ($D$) | `Time_Post` ($P$) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Month 1 | 24.1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| Month 2 | 23.8 | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | 0 | 0 |
| Month 18 | 25.2 | 18 | 0 | 0 |
| **Month 19 (Policy)** | **18.4** | **19** | **1** | **1** |
| Month 20 | 17.9 | 20 | 1 | 2 |
| $\dots$ | $\dots$ | $\dots$ | 1 | $\dots$ |
| Month 36 | 12.1 | 36 | 1 | 18 |

---

## 4. Running the Model via SPSS Menus

### Step 1: Open Linear Regression
Navigate to **Analyze > Regression > Linear...**

### Step 2: Assign Variables
* Move `Infection_Rate` into the **Dependent** box.
* Move `Time`, `Intervention`, and `Time_Post` into the **Independent(s)** box.
* Leave **Method** set to `Enter`.

```
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Linear Regression                                            |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
| Dependent:     [ Infection_Rate                           ]  |
|                                                              |
| Independents:  [ Time                                     ]  |
|                [ Intervention                             ]  |
|                [ Time_Post                                ]  |
|                                                              |
| Method:        [ Enter                                   v]  |
+--------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### Step 3: Configure Output Statistics
Click the **Statistics...** button on the right:
1. Ensure **Estimates** and **Model fit** are checked.
2. Check **95% Confidence intervals**.
3. Under **Residuals**, check **Durbin-Watson**.
4. Click **Continue**.

### Step 4: Optional Diagnostic Plots
Click the **Plots...** button on the right:
1. Move `*ZRESID` (standardized residuals) into the **Y** box.
2. Move `*ZPRED` (standardized predicted values) into the **X** box.
3. Check **Histogram** and **Normal probability plot**.
4. Click **Continue**, then click **OK** to run.

---

## 5. Interpreting the SPSS Output Tables

### A. Model Summary Table

| Model | $R$ | $R$ Square | Adjusted $R$ Square | Std. Error of the Estimate | Durbin-Watson |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | .942 | .887 | .876 | 1.142 | **1.895** |

* **Durbin-Watson Statistic:** Tests for first-order autocorrelation ($\text{AR}(1)$).
  * Values close to **2.0** indicate **no serial correlation** (independent errors).
  * Values below **1.5** suggest positive autocorrelation (errors are correlated over time, which can artificially deflate $p$-values).
  * A value of $1.895$ indicates that standard OLS assumptions are acceptable for this series.

### B. Coefficients Table

| Model | Unstandardized B | Std. Error | Standardized Beta | $t$ | Sig. ($p$) | 95% Confidence Interval (B) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **(Constant)** | 23.410 | 0.485 | | 48.27 | < .001 | [22.42, 24.40] |
| **`Time`** | 0.082 | 0.046 | 0.165 | 1.78 | .084 | [-0.012, 0.176] |
| **`Intervention`** | -4.850 | 0.742 | -0.612 | -6.54 | < .001 | [-6.36, -3.34] |
| **`Time_Post`** | -0.395 | 0.068 | -0.684 | -5.81 | < .001 | [-0.53, -0.26] |

### Practical Translation of Results:
1. **Baseline Trend (`Time` = $0.082$, $p = .084$):** Prior to the policy, infection rates were slightly increasing by $0.082$ units per month, though this slope was not statistically significant at the $\alpha = .05$ level.
2. **Immediate Effect (`Intervention` = $-4.850$, $p < .001$):** At Month 19, the intervention produced an immediate, statistically significant drop of $4.85$ infections per 100 patient days ($95\%\text{ CI: } [-6.36, -3.34]$).
3. **Trend Shift (`Time_Post` = $-0.395$, $p < .001$):** The rate of change shifted downward significantly by $0.395$ units per month post-intervention compared to the baseline trend.
4. **Overall Post-Intervention Slope:**
   $$\text{Post-Slope} = \beta_1 + \beta_3 = 0.082 + (-0.395) = -0.313 \text{ per month}$$
   Infections steadily decreased by approximately $0.31$ cases per month after the policy took effect.

---

## 6. What If the Durbin-Watson Statistic Fails?

If the Durbin-Watson statistic is $< 1.5$, standard regression standard errors are biased downward due to autocorrelation. SPSS offers two point-and-click remedies:

### Remedy 1: Generalized Linear Models with Autoregressive Errors
1. Navigate to **Analyze > Generalized Linear Models > Generalized Linear Models...**
2. In the **Repeated** tab, designate `Time` as the **Within-subject variable**.
3. Set the **Covariance Matrix structure** to **First-order autoregressive (AR1)**.
4. Set outcome and covariates as usual under the **Predictors** and **Model** tabs.

### Remedy 2: Time Series ARIMA Modeling
1. Go to **Analyze > Forecasting > Create Traditional Models...**
2. Under **Method**, select **ARIMA**.
3. Click **Criteria...** to specify an autoregressive component ($p=1$).
4. Add `Intervention` and `Time_Post` as transfer functions / independent predictors.

---

## 7. Generating the Final Plot in SPSS

A clear ITS publication graph displays observed points, the fitted trend lines, and the projected counterfactual path.

1. Go to **Transform > Compute Variable...** to create the counterfactual values:
   * Target Variable: `Counterfactual`
   * Numeric Expression: `23.410 + (0.082 * Time)` *(using your estimated $\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$)*
2. In the Linear Regression dialog, click **Save...** and check **Unstandardized Predicted Values** (`PRE_1`).
3. Open **Graphs > Chart Builder...**
4. Choose **Line** (Multiple Lines) or **Scatter/Dot** (Overlay Scatter).
5. Drag `Time` to the X-axis.
6. Overlay `Infection_Rate` (as dots), `PRE_1` (as a solid fitted line), and `Counterfactual` (as a dotted continuation past Month 19).
7. Add a reference line on the X-axis at $18.5$ via the Chart Editor to highlight the intervention launch.
